prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, enabling atomic frequency standards with fractional uncertainty at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks rest on a concrete idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, which cancels the light shift for thousands of atoms interrogated at once) followed by a long experimental road to 1e-18 fractional uncertainty. Performance has been reproduced and compared across JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB and NIST, which is the standard of evidence I trust most. The consequences are already scientific and not merely technical: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetre scales, tighter limits on drifting constants and on dark-matter couplings, relativistic geodesy, and the prospect of a redefinition of the second. Katori gave the concept and first demonstration, and Ye drove the instrument to record accuracy and stability, so a two-person award is clean. Recognition is timely because the technique is mature and still opening new measurements.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision metrology has been recognised repeatedly (combs 2005, ion-trap work 2012), so a committee could read lattice clocks as an incremental step on a well-honoured line, and as an instrument advance rather than a discovery of nature. Credit is also not perfectly tidy: Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and others in Paris and Boulder made decisive contributions. Ye's possible later candidacy for the thorium clock is a strategic complication. I think these are weaker than they look, because the new regime of control (many-atom quantum-limited interrogation) and the new science it enables are distinct from the earlier prizes.

responses.point: Lindroth also ranks lattice clocks first and values that the underlying atomic physics is clean and well understood, while asking whether the committee will treat optical clocks as a discovery of nature or as an instrument and metrology advance.
responses.response: I agree on the physics and on the two-person split, but I would not rest the case on whether it is a discovery in the narrow sense. Nobel's will allows an invention or discovery, and what matters is whether the measurement capability changes what can be learned. Millimetre-scale redshift, constant-variation limits and dark-matter searches are results of that kind. Where I would press you is on your worry that Ye's comb work overlaps with 2005. The comb is a tool the lattice clock uses; the magic-wavelength lattice, the spin-polarised many-atom interrogation and the stability engineering are separate contributions, and I would keep the citation worded around the lattice clock to make that clear.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a clean case of theory anticipating a new state of matter, followed by experiments reproduced across many groups, while admitting that the pairing mechanism is unresolved and the timing is arguably early.
responses.response: I accept that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiments is a strong story and that reproduction by many groups is real; that is why I keep B019 as an alternative. My reservation is the one you raise yourself: the object being honoured is a set of phases whose origin is still argued, and I know from rare-earth work how long it takes before a surprising observation becomes a settled, quantitatively understood effect. The credit also leaves out the experimental first author. A lattice clock has a quantitatively verified result today, with agreement between laboratories at the 1e-18 level. I would ask whether the committee gains by waiting a few years on twisted bilayers while the clock case is already complete.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, ranks IceCube first as an instrument-driven discovery that opened a new window, with a confirmed diffuse flux and source associations still at 3 to 4 sigma, and places lattice clocks second.
responses.response: I share your preference for instrument-driven discovery and I take the diffuse neutrino flux as solid. The difference is in what is settled. The flux is established, but the source identifications are below 5 sigma and the physical interpretation is still moving, whereas the lattice clock result is quantitatively reproduced by independent groups now. IceCube also has a collaboration-size and early-pioneer problem (AMANDA, Baikal, DUMAND) that makes two names harder to defend than Katori and Ye. I would like to hear from you whether Halzen and Spiering really cover the decisive credit; if they do, I regard B032 as the best non-AMO competitor, but I still place it behind the clocks on maturity of interpretation.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy first as an invention verified by direct demonstration that lets us see what could not be seen before, and ranks lattice clocks fourth, noting that overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes may affect appetite.
responses.response: I am sympathetic to the instrumentation argument, since my own priority is measurement methods that open new observations, and the microscope case is as mature as any. But the instrument case is stronger when the instrument has changed what questions physics itself can ask. Electron microscopy has transformed materials science and chemistry; the credit question also remains open because Krivanek and the STEM line are outside the three names, as you note. Lattice clocks sit more directly in physics (fundamental constants, relativity, dark matter). On overlap, I would say the 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured combs and single-ion control, not many-atom lattice interrogation, so I do not see the overlap as disqualifying.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the lattice clock only seventh, acknowledging the large importance for precision physics and clear two-person credit, but doubting whether the community sees it as a discovery or an engineering refinement, and noting overlap with earlier clock prizes.
responses.response: I respect that you weigh simple, general mechanisms most, and I would argue the magic-wavelength condition is exactly that: one clean criterion for cancelling the dominant systematic that then carries over to many species and geometries. The result is not an engineering refinement in the usual sense, since reaching 1e-18 required new physics-level understanding of blackbody shifts, collisional and tunnelling effects, and laser coherence. Where I agree with you is that the prize would be stronger if the citation is framed around that mechanism and its consequences, and I will propose wording that does so. I do not think the attribution is the weak point; it is probably the cleanest on the shortlist.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a second consecutive-era metrology prize on frequency standards after 2005 and 2012, or will prefer a different area of AMO physics (B050) this year.
How to weigh Lemonde, Ludlow and other early lattice-clock contributors against the Katori and Ye pair; I rely on memory for exact priority of the first Sr lattice-clock demonstrations.
If the thorium nuclear clock (not on this shortlist) matures, whether recognising Ye now would later complicate that recognition.
Whether B050 (Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger versus Zoller) can be given a defensible three-person allocation, since I proposed the three experimentalists but Zoller and Jaksch proposed the scheme.
statement.conflict_note: A possible personal connection to flag: during my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye is at JILA in the same community as Hall. I have no direct collaboration, supervision or institutional tie to Katori or Ye that I know of, and I do not consider this a recusal-level conflict, but the committee should know about it. For other shortlisted candidates, no specific conflict is apparent from my profile; my Lund quantum-information work is not directly tied to any credited name, and the Chalmers overlap through WACQT concerns a fellow committee member, not a candidate.
